tagline.text: Cradle of Independence: Santa Barbara Church, where the Visayan revolutionary government was proclaimed

children.text: Santa Barbara Church is an Augustinian church in the town of Santa Barbara, about 15 km north of Iloilo City. It is where the Visayan revolutionary government was proclaimed in 1898, and it is designated a National Historical Landmark and a National Cultural Treasure.
Santa Barbara Parish Church stands in the center of the town of Santa Barbara, about
15 km

north of Iloilo City. Unlike the famous churches of Molo and Jaro in the city, you have to head inland to reach it, but Wikipedia calls it the "Cradle of Independence" of Panay and the Visayas, which tells you how much it weighs in Philippine history. Wikipedia and OSM point to the same spot (about 10.83 N, 122.53 E).
The settlement was originally called Catmon and was a visita (mission station) of Jaro, until it became an independent parish in

with Saint Barbara as its patron. The present brick church was begun under the Augustinian friar Francisco Aguerria. Sources disagree on the start year, 1845 or 1849, and it is said to have been completed in 1878 by Fr. Calixto Fernandez. Construction relied on parishioners' taxes and the colonial forced-labor system, and stone and timber were brought from nearby towns.
The church became famous in 1898. According to Wikipedia's entry on the town, on
November 17, 1898

the Philippine flag was raised here for the first time outside Luzon, and the Visayan revolutionary government led by President Roque Lopez and General Martin Delgado was proclaimed. The revolutionaries used the church as headquarters and garrison and the neighboring convent as a military hospital. For this reason the church and convent were designated together as a National Historical Landmark and a National Cultural Treasure.

It also helps to know a little of the town's history. Fr. Felipe Ruiz became parish priest in 1762, and Fr. Mateo Rodriguez is said to have continued the construction from 1855 to 1873. After the revolution, General Martin Delgado surrendered to US forces on
February 2, 1901

and later became governor of Iloilo. The town had about 68,000 people in the 2024 census, and every November 17 it holds the Kahilwayan Festival to commemorate this history. The town also has an irrigation dam built in 1926, the Centennial Museum and Convention Center, and a Catmon tree beside the municipal hall. The building has a cruciform plan with a neoclassical facade. The plain facade is divided by four pairs of Tuscan pilasters, niches on either side of the arched main portal hold statues of Christ and Mary, and above the three arches of the upper level the emblems of the Pope and the Augustinians are carved in high relief. A statue of the patron, Saint Barbara, sits in the niche at the very top. The convent is described as having Moorish elements. Rather than expecting an ornate Baroque church, think of it as a modest brick church and the history stored inside it. The church stands close to the central plaza, so in an hour or two you can see the exterior, the plaza and the convent surroundings. It pairs well with Molo Church and Jaro Cathedral for a one-day church circuit. Note, however, that Wikipedia's infobox lists the church's status as "under restoration," so it is safest to check by phone or on the parish Facebook page before you go.

Four pairs of Tuscan pilasters divide the facade, and niches on either side of the arched portal hold statues of Christ and Mary. Three stained glass windows on the upper level show that a choir loft lies inside. In the afternoon the sun lights the facade, which makes for good photos.

blocks.title: Emblems of the Pope and the Augustinians

children.text: Above the arches of the upper level, the symbols of the Pope and the Augustinian order are carved in high relief. They are a trace of the church's Augustinian parish past, and comparing them with other Augustinian churches in Panay, such as Miagao and Molo, is part of the fun.
In the niche at the top of the trefoil-shaped pediment stands a statue of the patron, Saint Barbara. Both the church and the town take their names from this saint, whose feast day is
December 4
every year.

The convent beside the church is described as having Moorish elements, and it served as a military hospital during the 1898 revolution. Whether the interior is open, and when, must be confirmed with the parish, but even from outside you can sense the scale of a convent built as one body with the church.

blocks.title: Site of the Visayan revolutionary government

children.text: It is said that the revolution led by General Delgado on
November 17, 1898
centered on this place. The church was the revolutionaries' garrison and the convent was a hospital. For anyone who knows Philippine revolutionary history, simply standing here is meaningful.

Santa Barbara Plaza near the church is where the revolutionary government was inaugurated in 1898, and it has a bandstand built in 1925, a Rizal Monument and other memorials. It is within walking distance of the church, so see them together.

The church and convent were declared a National Historical Landmark in 1990–1991 and a National Cultural Treasure by the National Museum in 2013. The 2013 restoration is said to have cost about 50 million pesos, and a historical marker has been installed. Sources differ slightly on the designation years, so remember it as "the early 1990s."
Every year on
November 17

the town holds the Kahilwayan Festival with street dancing, cultural performances and reenactments involving General Delgado. The area around the church is liveliest at this time. Roads get congested and crowds are large, so go early.
Set out from Iloilo City. Santa Barbara is about
15 km
from the city, and you can reach it along Benigno S. Aquino Jr. Avenue by jeepney, bus, van, taxi or tricycle.
Arrive at Santa Barbara Church and take your time over the pilasters, niches, emblems and the saint at the top of the facade. Entry to the church is generally known to be free.
If the parish office is open, ask whether the convent and church interior are accessible. The office is reported to be closed on Mondays.
At the nearby Santa Barbara Plaza (Victory Plaza), see the bandstand and the Rizal Monument and imagine the proclamation of the revolutionary government.
Have lunch in the town center. Ask locally for long-established restaurants.
Return to the city and visit Molo Church and Jaro Cathedral to complete the church circuit.
Mass times can change from week to week, so confirm with the parish before visiting. Keep quiet during Mass and dress with shoulders and knees covered.

items.title: Revolution history route
items.subtitle: The church, the plaza and a walk around town

children.text: Start at Santa Barbara Plaza and see the bandstand built in 1925 and the Rizal Monument. This is where the revolutionary government was inaugurated in 1898.
Walk to the church, study the facade, emblems and saint at the top, and walk around the exterior while remembering that the convent served as a military hospital.
Head toward the Catmon tree near the municipal hall and the Centennial Museum and Convention Center to check the town's history displays. Confirm locally whether they are open.
The Iloilo Golf and Country Club in Barangay San Sebastian is a drive away; look at it from the outside, or skip it if you are short of time.
If you visit on November 17, check the Kahilwayan event schedule in the municipal news first.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Iloilo International Airport (ILO). The flight takes about
1 hour 10 minutes
; check schedules and fares by airline when booking.
Iloilo International Airport lies next to the town of Santa Barbara on the Cabatuan side, so you can also see the church first before heading into the city.

items.title: From Iloilo City to Santa Barbara

children.text: It is about
15 km
north of Iloilo City, and Benigno S. Aquino Jr. Avenue is the main route. Jeepneys, buses, vans, taxis and tricycles are reported to run there.
Exact fares and boarding points can change over time, so check at the terminal or your accommodation. A taxi or Grab is convenient, but negotiate the round-trip waiting fee in advance.
The church, plaza and municipal hall are within walking distance of one another. Take a tricycle for places a little farther away.
The church can be visited all year, but the dry season is best for the outdoor plaza and the exterior.

If you are interested in history, time your visit with the Kahilwayan Festival on November 17 or Saint Barbara's feast day on December 4, when events are held, but expect crowds and check the schedule in advance.

The church is easy to visit as a day trip from Iloilo City, so most travelers stay in city hotels. Because it is near the airport, if you have an early flight or a late arrival you could stay near the airport and see the church first.

It is simplest to eat at a restaurant in the town center or back in the city. Enjoy local food such as the city's famous La Paz batchoy in the city. Menus and prices at restaurants in town are best checked on the day. The opening hours of the Centennial Museum can change, so confirm them locally, and the most rewarding plan is to walk slowly around the town plaza along with your church visit.
Before visiting, check whether the church is open and the Mass times by calling the parish at (033) 523-7928 or on its Facebook page, SBParishChurch. Wikipedia lists it as "under restoration."
The parish office is reported to be open Tuesday to Sunday, 9 AM to 12 noon and 1 PM to 5 PM, and closed on Mondays. Check the latest notice.
Masses are reported to be at about 5:30 AM and 5 PM on weekdays, with an 8 AM Mass on Sundays as well, but they may change week to week.
Dress with shoulders and knees covered, and refrain from taking photos during Mass.
Combining it with Molo Church and Jaro Cathedral on the same day makes for efficient travel.
During the Kahilwayan Festival on November 17 there may be traffic control, so set out early.
There is little shade around the church, so bring a hat and water.
There is information that the church is under restoration, so the doors may be closed. Check with the parish before you go.
Access to the church interior and convent depends on the parish's circumstances.
During Mass, refrain from entering for sightseeing and from taking photos.
Transport fares change over time, so confirm them before boarding.
During festivals watch out for pickpockets and carry your belongings in front of you.
In the rainy season, check typhoon news.
